explanation: Judges 15:13 records that the men of Judah bound Samson with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock. Seven fresh bowstrings not yet dried is a detail from the Delilah story later (Judges 16:7), not this occasion (near_passage). Bronze chains are how the Philistines later shackled him in Gaza (Judges 16:21), a different context entirely (wrong_scope). Ropes braided from hair also belong to the Delilah context, not the men of Judah (near_passage).

content: After the battle with his unusual weapon, Samson was exhausted and desperately thirsty. How did God answer him, and what was that place named?
options: God split open a hollow place and water came out; that place was called En-hakkore
God caused water to flow from the jawbone of the donkey itself; that place was called Ramath-lehi
God sent ravens to bring him water; that place was called En-hakkore
God opened a spring in a rock; that place was called Ramath-lehi
explanation: Judges 15:19 records that God split open the hollow place that is at Lehi, and water came from it; Samson drank, and his spirit returned, so the place was named En-hakkore ('the spring of him who called'), which is at Lehi to this day. The option that water flowed from the jawbone itself is a common misreading, and Ramath-lehi ('the hill of the jawbone') is the name of where he threw the jawbone in verse 17, not the name of the spring (common_misconception). Ravens bringing water is confused with the story of the prophet Elijah (1 Kings 17), which has nothing to do with Samson (wrong_scope). Water springing from a rock recalls Moses' miracle at Horeb (Exodus 17), and the name Ramath-lehi is again incorrectly assigned to the spring (wrong_scope).

content: Samson's riddle was based on a private experience that only he knew about. Why could the young men not solve the riddle on their own without an inside tip?
options: It was based on bees making a hive in the carcass of a lion he had killed, which no one had witnessed
It was based on finding gold hidden in a cave, which he kept completely secret
It was based on a strange dream about a lion that God had given to him alone
It was based on a secret oracle that a priest had spoken to him alone
explanation: Judges 14:6–9 shows that Samson killed the lion when he was alone and told no one; later he found a swarm of bees and honey in its carcass. The riddle — 'Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet' (14:14) — was based entirely on this secret experience, so no one could guess it unless his wife disclosed it. Gold hidden in a cave is a fabricated detail; the source of the riddle was the lion and the honey, not hidden treasure (wrong_detail). A dream about a lion is wrong because this was a real event Samson personally experienced, not a vision or dream (common_misconception). A secret oracle from a priest is also a fabricated detail; the text mentions no priest in connection with this riddle (wrong_detail).

content: When surrounded at Gaza, what did Samson do with the city gate at midnight before leaving?
options: He tore off the city gate with its two posts and carried them to the top of a hill
He burned the city gate and then fled outside
He broke down the city wall with a large wooden beam
He climbed over the city wall by means of a rope
explanation: Judges 16:3 records that Samson took hold of the doors of the gate of the city and the two posts, pulled them up, bar and all, and put them on his shoulders and carried them to the top of the hill that is in front of Hebron. The option 'burned the city gate' is an incorrect detail because the text says he tore them out, not burned them (wrong_detail). 'Broke down the city wall with a wooden beam' confuses this with a general siege action not found in this passage (wrong_scope). 'Climbed over the wall by means of a rope' contradicts the extraordinary strength described (common_misconception).

content: After capturing Samson, what work did the Philistines make him do in prison?
options: Draw water from a deep well
Cut stones to build a city wall
Grind at the mill in the prison
Row a boat on the great sea
explanation: Judges 16:21 records that the Philistines seized Samson, gouged out his eyes, brought him down to Gaza, bound him with bronze shackles, and he ground at the mill in the prison. 'Draw water from a deep well' is a different form of forced labor not found in the text (wrong_detail). 'Cut stones to build a city wall' suggests general prisoner labor but is an incorrect detail (wrong_scope). 'Row a boat on the great sea' is completely out of context (common_misconception).

content: Samson's final catastrophe occurred when the Philistines gathered to offer sacrifice to which of their gods?
options: Baal
Dagon
Molech
Ashtaroth
explanation: Judges 16:23 records that the lords of the Philistines gathered to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon their god and to rejoice. 'Baal' is a Canaanite god the Israelites often worshiped in this book, but is not the god of the Philistines in this passage (near_passage). 'Molech' is the god of the Ammonites — the wrong people group (wrong_scope). 'Ashtaroth' is also mentioned in Judges but is not the god worshiped in the scene of the collapsing temple (wrong_detail).

content: In Micah's house, who was appointed as priest before the Levite arrived?
options: One of Micah's younger brothers
One of Micah's servants
A stranger passing through
One of Micah's sons
explanation: Judges 17:5 records that Micah ordained one of his sons, who became his priest. 'One of his brothers' is an incorrect family relationship compared to the text (wrong_detail). 'One of his servants' confuses the household role but names the wrong person (near_passage). 'A stranger passing through' is confused with the Levite who arrived later in verses 7–12 (wrong_scope).

content: According to the text, why did the Philistine lords come to Delilah to discover the secret of Samson's strength?
options: They threatened to burn down her father's house if she refused
Each of them promised to give her 1,100 pieces of silver
They promised to give her in marriage to the wealthiest lord in Philistia
They pledged to appoint her as a priestess of the temple of Dagon
explanation: Judges 16:5 records that the lords of the Philistines said to Delilah: 'Seduce him, and see where his great strength lies… and we will each give you 1,100 pieces of silver.' 'Threatened to burn down her father's house' is almost right, since a burning threat appears in the text, but it was directed at Samson in 15:6, not at Delilah (near_passage). 'Promised to give her in marriage to the wealthiest lord' is a fabricated motive not found in the passage (wrong_detail). 'Appoint her as a priestess of the temple of Dagon' borrows the temple context from later in the chapter but misrepresents the actual event (wrong_scope).

content: In the first two times Delilah pressed Samson, what did he successively say could be used to bind him and make him weak?
options: New ropes that had never been used, then seven fresh bowstrings
Seven locks of his hair woven into a loom, then fresh bowstrings
Seven fresh bowstrings, then new ropes that had never been used
Bronze chains on his feet, then seven fresh bowstrings
explanation: Judges 16:7 records that Samson said if they bound him with seven fresh bowstrings (moist cords) that had not been dried, he would become weak; verse 11 records that the next time he said to use new ropes that had never been used. 'New ropes first and then bowstrings' reverses the order of the two attempts (wrong_detail). 'Seven locks of his hair woven into a loom' is the third attempt in verse 13, not the first two (near_passage). 'Bronze chains on his feet' is how the Philistines actually bound him after his capture in verse 21, not what Samson said (wrong_scope).

content: According to the text, what did Micah's mother do with the eleven hundred pieces of silver that Micah returned to her?
options: Had all eleven hundred pieces cast into one large carved image
Took two hundred pieces and had a carved image and a cast image made
Dedicated all of it to the priest at the temple in Shiloh
Took two hundred pieces to buy an ephod and household gods
explanation: Judges 17:4 records that Micah's mother took two hundred pieces of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a cast image, which were placed in Micah's house. 'All eleven hundred pieces cast' exaggerates the amount used compared to the actual two hundred in the text (wrong_detail). 'Dedicated all to the priest at Shiloh' contradicts the text, since the silver was used to make images for a private household (wrong_scope). 'Bought an ephod and household gods' is almost correct since an ephod and teraphim do appear in Micah's house in verse 5, but they are not what was purchased with these two hundred pieces of silver (near_passage).

content: The young Levite who came to stay at Micah's house was originally from which city?
options: Shiloh in Ephraim
Gaza in Philistia
Bethlehem in Judah
Hebron in Judah
explanation: Judges 17:7 records that there was a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah who was looking for a place to stay and came to Micah's house in the hill country of Ephraim. 'Shiloh in Ephraim' is almost correct since Ephraim is indeed where Micah's house was located, but that is the destination, not the Levite's hometown (near_passage). 'Gaza in Philistia' crosses over into the context of Samson in chapter 16 (wrong_scope). 'Hebron in Judah' has the right territory of Judah but the wrong city (wrong_detail).

content: Compared to Delilah's previous attempts, what caused Samson to truly lose his strength and not realize that the LORD had departed from him?
options: His seven locks of hair were tightly woven into a loom so he could not move
The hair on his head was shaved, breaking his Nazirite vow so the LORD left him
He was bound with new ropes so his sinews of strength could not break free
The Philistines gouged out his eyes first so he lost his bearings and could not resist
explanation: Judges 16:17 records that Samson revealed that no razor had ever come upon his head because he had been a Nazirite consecrated to God from birth; verses 19–20 record that after his hair was shaved, his strength left him and the LORD had departed from him without his knowing. 'Seven locks of hair woven into a loom' is almost correct since this was the third attempt in verses 13–14, but at that point his hair had not yet been shaved so his strength remained (near_passage). 'Bound with new ropes' is almost correct since this method genuinely appears in verses 11–12, but he snapped them easily (wrong_detail). 'Eyes gouged out first' reverses the sequence, because the gouging out of his eyes occurred after he had already lost his strength and been captured in verse 21 (wrong_scope).

content: When inviting the Levite to stay as his priest, what wages did Micah offer, and what conclusion did he draw from the arrangement?
options: Ten pieces of silver per year plus clothing and food; he believed the LORD would bless him
One hundred pieces of silver per year plus clothing and food; he believed he would become a judge
Ten pieces of silver as a one-time payment plus housing and servants; he believed he would defeat the Danites
Two hundred pieces of silver per year plus a carved image; he believed he would establish a great temple
explanation: Judges 17:10 records that Micah invited the Levite to be a father and priest to him, promising ten pieces of silver per year, a set of garments, and food; verse 13 records Micah saying that now he knew the LORD would be good to him because he had a Levite as priest. 'One hundred pieces of silver… become a judge' is wrong in both the amount and the conclusion, since there is no aspiration to become a judge anywhere in the text (wrong_detail). 'Ten pieces of silver as a one-time payment… defeat the Danites' has the correct number ten but the wrong payment terms, and crosses over into the Danites seizing the idols in chapter 18 (near_passage). 'Two hundred pieces of silver… establish a great temple' takes the number two hundred from the silver used to cast the image in verse 4 and inflates the conclusion into founding a temple (wrong_scope).

content: In Judges 18, which tribe was seeking a territory to settle in because it had not yet received an inheritance among the tribes of Israel?
options: The tribe of Dan
The tribe of Benjamin
The tribe of Judah
The tribe of Ephraim
explanation: Judges 18:1 states: 'In those days the tribe of the Danites was seeking for itself an inheritance to live in, for until then no inheritance among the tribes of Israel had fallen to them.' So the correct answer is the tribe of Dan. Benjamin is the tribe associated with the incident at Gibeah in chapters 19–20, not the tribe seeking land (near_passage). Judah had already received a clear inheritance beforehand (wrong_detail). Ephraim is where Micah lived (chapters 17–18) but was not the tribe seeking land (wrong_scope).

content: When the tribe of Dan sent spies to scout the land, at whose house did they stop and spend the night in the hill country of Ephraim?
options: Micah's house
Gideon's house
Jephthah's house
Abdon's house
explanation: Judges 18:2–3 states that the Dan spies came to the hill country of Ephraim and 'came to the house of Micah and lodged there.' So the correct answer is Micah's house. Gideon was a judge from an earlier story and has no connection to this passage (wrong_scope). Jephthah was also a different judge who does not appear in chapter 18 (wrong_scope). Abdon was a judge mentioned in the book but is not a character in this story (wrong_scope).

content: Why did the Dan spies consider the city of Laish an easy target to seize?
options: The people there lived securely, without defense, and far from the Sidonians, with no one to rescue them
The people there had just been defeated in battle and had no soldiers left to resist
The city had no walls, so the Danite forces could rush in at any time
The people there had voluntarily surrendered and invited the Danites to rule over them
explanation: Judges 18:7, 28 describes the people of Laish as living 'quiet and unsuspecting, lacking nothing' in the manner of the Sidonians, and 'far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone,' so there was no one to rescue them. That is why the city was easy to capture. The option 'just defeated in battle' adds details not found in the text (wrong_detail). The option 'no walls' sounds plausible, but the reason the text gives is the people's complacency and isolation, not the absence of walls (common_misconception). The option 'voluntarily surrendered' reverses the facts: the Danites attacked by surprise and burned the city (wrong_detail).

content: When six hundred Danites passed by Micah's house, what did the five spies do with the young priest who was serving there?
options: They invited the priest to go with them as priest for an entire tribe rather than for one household
They forced the priest to be silent and then drove him out of Micah's house
They killed the priest in order to take the idols and the ephod
They paid Micah a ransom to lawfully purchase the priest
explanation: Judges 18:19 records the Danites saying to the priest: 'Is it better for you to be priest to the house of one man, or to be priest to a tribe and clan in Israel?' and 'the heart of the priest was glad.' So they persuaded the priest to come with them. The option 'forced to be silent and driven out' is wrong because they invited him rather than expelled him (wrong_detail). The option 'killed the priest' contradicts the text, since the priest willingly went with them and brought the sacred objects along (wrong_detail). The option 'paid a lawful ransom to Micah' is wrong because they took everything without paying, causing Micah to pursue them to reclaim his property (common_misconception).

content: After capturing the city of Laish, what new name did the Danites give it?
options: Dan
Lehi
Mizpah
Bethel
explanation: Judges 18:29 states: 'they named the city Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor.' So the city was renamed Dan. Lehi is a place associated with the story of Samson and is unrelated to this passage (wrong_scope). Mizpah is the assembly point of Israel in chapters 20–21 and was not the name given to this city (near_passage). Bethel was where the ark of the covenant was kept at that time but was not the new name of Laish (wrong_detail).

content: What does the conclusion of Judges 18 tell us about the worship of the Danites at their new city?
options: They set up the carved image for themselves throughout the time the house of God was at Shiloh
They destroyed the image and returned to worship at the tabernacle in Shiloh
They set up an altar to Baal following the example of the surrounding nations
They kept only the ephod and discarded the carved images for fear of breaking the commandment
explanation: Judges 18:30-31 records that the Danites 'set up the carved image' and appointed Jonathan's descendants as priests, keeping Micah's carved image 'all the time that the house of God was at Shiloh.' The question requires distinguishing: the text emphasizes that they maintained idolatry while the legitimate sanctuary still existed at Shiloh — a spiritual contrast. The option 'destroyed the image and returned to Shiloh' reverses the meaning of the narrative (common_misconception). The option 'set up an altar to Baal' adds details not present; the text speaks of Micah's carved image, not Baal (wrong_detail). The option 'kept only the ephod and discarded the images' is incorrect because verse 30 emphasizes that the carved image itself was set up and retained (wrong_detail).

content: The story in Judges 19 opens with a Levite living in what region who went to bring back his concubine after she had left him and returned to her father's house in Bethlehem?
options: The remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim
The plains of Jericho
The hill country of Hebron
The coast of Joppa
explanation: Judges 19:1 states: 'there was a certain Levite sojourning in the remote parts of the hill country of Ephraim, who took to himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.' Therefore the Levite lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim. Jericho is a city he later passed by without stopping to lodge (near_passage). Hebron is a city in Judah, not where he lived (wrong_detail). Joppa is a coastal city unrelated to this story (wrong_scope).

content: On the return journey, why did the Levite refuse his servant's suggestion to lodge in the city of Jebus (that is, Jerusalem)?
options: Because it was a city of foreigners, so he wanted to continue on to a city of Israel
Because it was already completely dark and the gates of Jebus had been shut
Because he feared that the people of Jebus would come out and plunder his whole company
Because he had already arranged to spend the night at the house of an acquaintance in Jebus
explanation: Judges 19:11-12 records the Levite saying: 'We will not turn aside into the city of foreigners, who do not belong to the people of Israel, but we will pass on to Gibeah.' Therefore the reason was that Jebus was a city of foreigners. The option 'the gates were already shut' adds details not present in the text; in fact there was still enough daylight to continue on to Gibeah (wrong_detail). The option 'feared being plundered' is not the reason the text gives, which was a matter of ethnic and covenant identity (common_misconception). The option 'had arranged with an acquaintance' is entirely wrong, since upon arriving at Gibeah he had to sit in the town square because no one offered to take him in (wrong_detail).

content: At Gibeah, who was the only person willing to receive the Levite and invite him into their home for the night?
options: An old man who was originally from the hill country of Ephraim and was sojourning in Gibeah
An elder of Benjamin who had lived in Gibeah for many years
A priest who happened to be passing through the town square
A relative of his concubine who had come from Bethlehem
explanation: Judges 19:16-20 records that 'an old man was coming from his work in the field at evening... He was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he was sojourning in Gibeah' — and this man invited the Levite into his home. He was therefore an old man originally from Ephraim who was sojourning there. The option 'an elder of Benjamin who had lived there for many years' is close in location but wrong in origin: he was from Ephraim, not a native Benjaminite (wrong_detail). The option 'a priest' introduces a character not present in the text (wrong_detail). The option 'a relative of his concubine' confuses this with the detail about her father in Bethlehem from the preceding section (near_passage).

content: After the tragedy at Gibeah, what did the Levite do to shock all Israel and compel them to act?
options: He cut his concubine's body into twelve pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel
He brought the body to the tabernacle at Shiloh to testify against the atrocity
He called the elders to assemble at Mizpah to judge the people of Gibeah
He wrote a letter recounting the atrocity and sent messengers to read it to the tribes
explanation: Judges 19:29 states: 'he took a knife, and taking hold of his concubine he divided her, limb by limb, into twelve pieces, and sent her throughout all the territory of Israel.' Therefore the act was cutting the body into twelve pieces and sending them out. The question requires distinguishing the inciting action (chapter 19) from subsequent events: the assembly 'at Mizpah' is a consequence described in chapter 20, not something the Levite did at the end of chapter 19 (wrong_scope). The option 'brought the body to the tabernacle at Shiloh' substitutes the location and manner with details not found in the text (wrong_detail). The option 'wrote a letter and sent messengers' replaces the viscerally shocking act with a far gentler means of communication, contrary to the text (common_misconception).

content: When the people of Israel heard about the crime that took place at Gibeah, at what place did all Israel assemble as one man before the LORD?
options: Mizpah
Shiloh
Bethel
Gilgal
explanation: Judges 20:1 records that the congregation gathered 'as one man at Mizpah before the LORD.' Shiloh was where the tabernacle was located at that time but was not the place of this assembly (near_passage). Bethel is where the people later went up to inquire of God (Judges 20:18), not the initial gathering place (near_passage). Gilgal is associated with the time of Joshua and not with this event (wrong_scope).

content: Among the soldiers of the tribe of Benjamin, there was a special group who favored which hand and were exceptionally skilled at slinging stones?
options: Left-handed
Right-handed
Both hands
Right hand was dominant
explanation: Judges 20:16 describes seven hundred chosen men who were all 'left-handed,' every one of whom could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. Right-handed is the direct opposite of what the text says (wrong_detail). 'Both hands' confuses this group with descriptions of other elite warriors elsewhere in the Old Testament (common_misconception). 'Right hand was dominant' invents a detail not found in the verse (wrong_detail).

content: When the people of Israel inquired of God as to which tribe should go up first to fight against Benjamin, why did they receive an answer designating Judah?
options: Because God designated Judah to go up first
Because Judah had the largest army
Because Judah was geographically closest to Gibeah
Because Judah volunteered to lead the battle
explanation: Judges 20:18 records that the people went up to Bethel to inquire, and the LORD answered: 'Judah shall go up first.' This was God's designation, not based on troop numbers (wrong_detail) — the text does not say Judah had the most soldiers. The geographical argument that Judah was nearest to Gibeah is not mentioned and is a false inference (wrong_detail). The notion that Judah 'volunteered' confuses this passage with Judges 1:1–2, where Judah was likewise designated to go first rather than self-selected (near_passage).

content: In the first two days of battle against the tribe of Benjamin, what outcome did the people of Israel experience?
options: Both days they were defeated with very heavy losses
The first day they were defeated; the second day they won a great victory
Both days they were victorious but advanced very slowly
The first day they won a great victory; the second day they were defeated
explanation: Judges 20:21 records that on the first day Benjamin killed 22,000 Israelites, and verse 25 records that on the second day they killed another 18,000 — meaning Israel was defeated on both days. 'First day defeated, second day victorious' is wrong because the victory only came on the third day (wrong_detail). 'Both days victorious' directly contradicts the text (wrong_detail). 'First day victorious, second day defeated' reverses the actual sequence of events (wrong_detail).

content: On the third day, what tactic finally enabled the people of Israel to defeat the forces of Benjamin at Gibeah?
options: They set an ambush and then feigned retreat to lure the enemy out of the city
They besieged the city and cut off its water supply until the enemy surrendered
They launched a direct frontal attack at night while the enemy was fast asleep
They divided their forces into three columns and simultaneously struck the city
explanation: Judges 20:29–32, 36 records that Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah, then the main force feigned retreat to draw the Benjaminites away from the city, after which the ambush troops rushed in and struck it. By contrast, besieging and cutting off the water supply is a tactic from other battles in biblical history but not this one (wrong_detail). 'Attacking at night while the enemy slept' is confused with Gideon's strategy in Judges 7 (near_passage). 'Dividing into three columns to strike simultaneously' also echoes Gideon's three companies and not the ambush-and-lure plan described here (near_passage). A careful reading of the text is needed to distinguish this ambush-with-feigned-retreat from other tactics in Judges.

content: After their victory, what did the Israelites do to the cities of the tribe of Benjamin?
options: Put the inhabitants to the sword, killed the livestock, and set the cities on fire
Took the people captive and made them forced laborers
Spared the cities and only collected tribute
Drove the people out of the cities and took them for themselves
explanation: Judges 20:48 records that Israel turned back against Benjamin and struck with the sword all the inhabitants of the cities, along with the livestock and everything they found, and they set all the cities on fire. 'Taking captives as forced laborers' does not appear in the text—it directly contradicts the total destruction carried out (wrong_detail). 'Sparing the cities and collecting tribute' stands entirely contrary to the severity of the punishment described (wrong_detail). 'Driving out the people and occupying the cities' is also incorrect, since the cities were burned rather than captured and held (wrong_detail).

content: At Mizpah, the Israelites swore an oath that would later put the tribe of Benjamin at risk of extinction. What was that oath?
options: No one would give his daughter in marriage to a Benjaminite
No one would engage in trade or commerce with a Benjaminite
No one would allow a Benjaminite to live in his city
No one would make a peace treaty with a Benjaminite
explanation: Judges 21:1 records that the people had sworn at Mizpah: 'None of us shall give his daughter in marriage to Benjamin.' It was precisely this oath that threatened the tribe with extinction due to the shortage of wives. 'Prohibiting trade' is not the content of the oath (wrong_detail). 'Prohibiting a Benjaminite from residing in one's city' is an inference not found in the verse (wrong_detail). 'Prohibiting a peace treaty' sounds plausible in the aftermath of war but is not the oath that was recorded (true_but_off).

content: To find wives for the surviving Benjaminites, the Israelites noted a city that had not come up to Mizpah for the assembly. What did they do to that city?
options: They destroyed Jabesh-gilead, sparing only 400 virgins
They destroyed Jabesh-gilead and took all the women captive
They fined Jabesh-gilead by requiring them to hand over 400 virgins
They destroyed Gibeah, sparing only 400 virgins
explanation: Judges 21:8-12 records that because Jabesh-gilead had not come up to Mizpah, the people sent 12,000 warriors to destroy the city, putting to death all the men and every woman who had lain with a man, but sparing 400 young virgins and bringing them to Shiloh. 'Taking all the women captive' is incorrect because only the virgins were kept—the rest were killed (wrong_detail). 'Fining them by requiring them to hand over people' is incorrect because the city was utterly destroyed, not merely required to surrender individuals (wrong_detail). 'Destroying Gibeah' confuses the location—Gibeah was the site of the original crime in chapters 19–20, whereas the city destroyed for its absence from the assembly was Jabesh-gilead (near_passage). Careful reading is required to distinguish the specific numbers and the correct place name.

content: Since the number of virgins from Jabesh-gilead was still insufficient, at what occasion in Shiloh was the second plan to provide wives for the Benjaminites carried out?
options: During the yearly feast when the young women came out to dance
On the Sabbath when the people gathered for worship
During the festival of presenting the firstborn to the LORD
During the harvest season when the young women went out to the fields
explanation: Judges 21:19-21 records that there was a yearly feast of the LORD at Shiloh, and the Benjaminites were instructed to hide in the vineyards and seize the young women who came out to dance as wives. The Sabbath is not the occasion mentioned in the text (wrong_detail). The 'festival of presenting the firstborn' is a different observance prescribed in the law and has no connection to this context (wrong_scope). 'The harvest season when the women went out to work in the fields' is incorrect because the text specifies that the young women came out to dance during the feast, not to perform agricultural work (wrong_detail).

content: The book of Judges closes with what observation about the condition of the Israelites at that time?
options: There was no king in Israel; everyone did what was right in his own eyes
The people wholeheartedly obeyed the law of the LORD
The elders governed the people with justice
The people lived in peace and safety under a righteous king
explanation: Judges 21:25 states: 'In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes,' summarizing the spiritual chaos of the era. 'Wholeheartedly obeying the law' stands in complete contrast to the actual state of disobedience described throughout the book (wrong_detail). 'Elders governing with justice' does not reflect the state of anarchy depicted in the text (wrong_detail). 'Living in peace under a righteous king' is incorrect because the very verse declares 'there was no king' (wrong_detail).
